definition.text: The build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH.

facts.text: It happens when a proton donor is added: an acid such as nitric, sulfuric or carbonic acid, or a compound such as aluminium sulfate that releases protons in the soil.
It also happens when base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium are leached from the soil.
It begins naturally as lichens and algae break down rock surfaces, and with time and weathering soils in natural ecosystems grow more acidic.
Soils start out acid and stay so when their parent materials are low in basic cations; acid rain, agriculture and pollution speed acidification up.
It leaves fewer available nutrients, more toxic elements and weaker biological functions such as nitrogen fixation.
Acidification helps alkaline soils but degrades land when it cuts crop productivity and biological activity and leaves soil more open to contamination and erosion.
It is most common in Southeast Asia, the Amazon Rainforest, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern United States, each with its own causes.
Surface liming, less fertilizer and irrigation can prevent it.

title: Acid rain and soil

definition.text: Rain or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, mainly from sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants, which acidifies the soils it falls on.

facts.text: Unpolluted rain is already acidic, around pH 5.0–5.5, from carbonic acid; acid rain is defined as below pH 5 and averages 4–5, with readings well below 2.4 reported in industrial areas.
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, from lightning, volcanoes or human emissions, are converted in the troposphere into sulfuric and nitric acids.
Fossil fuels are the largest human source of sulfuric gases and motor exhaust the largest of nitrogen oxides.
Hydrogen ions in acid rain exchange for calcium and magnesium on clay, leaching these base cations and mobilizing aluminium, which harms sensitive trees such as sugar maple.
Low pH kills sensitive soil microbes by denaturing their enzymes, collapsing functions such as decomposition and hurting plants that depend on microbes for nutrients.
Snow holds more nitric than sulfuric acid, so a spring meltwater pulse, up to 50% of annual precipitation, can sharply but briefly lower the pH of drainage water.
Soils buffer part of the acid: adsorbing sulfate releases OH−, and organic-rich forest floor horizons cut the H+ load reaching mineral horizons below.
Since the 1970s regulations such as the US Clean Air Act have cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions, reducing acid rain, as improving pH in Ontario lakes showed.

related: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
notes: Extended in gap-fill from the crawled Acid rain page; first drafted on Soil acidification#Acid rain.

definition.text: Acidification of soil by living things, as plant roots and decaying plant remains release protons and organic acids.

facts.text: Plant roots release protons and organic acids to chemically weather soil minerals.
Litter acidifies the O horizon more under conifers such as pine, spruce and fir, which return fewer base cations than deciduous trees, though such pH differences often preexisted the vegetation.
Calcium held in living biomass also strongly affects soil pH, by an amount that varies between species.

definition.text: Rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them, such as granite and sulfide-rich shale, coal and marine clay.

facts.text: Granites and allied igneous rocks are called 'acidic' because their abundant free quartz yields silicic acid on weathering; they are also low in calcium and magnesium.
Sulfide-rich shale and coal produce sulfuric acid, much stronger than silicic acid, when hydrated and oxidised; many coal soils are too acidic for vigorous plant growth.
Marine clays are often sulfide-rich and become very acidic if drained to an oxidising state.

definition.text: The lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers.

facts.text: Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones such as ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate and ammonium nitrate most of all; urea and compost acidify less.
Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify.
Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH.
Nitrification of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil.
Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation; sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.
Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied; nitrate-only fertilizers such as calcium or potassium nitrate do not acidify and can slightly raise pH.
Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming but many manures are not.

definition.text: The harm acidification does to plants and soil organisms, from stunted roots to lost biological diversity.

facts.text: Plants develop smaller, less durable roots with damaged tips, reduced height, poorer germination and stunted growth overall.
It reduces microbial and macrofaunal diversity and is directly linked to declines in endangered plant species.
Leaching of base cations raises the availability of toxic ions such as aluminium, whose toxicity inhibits root growth.
Leaves yellowing between the veins can signal it, though alkaline or nutrient-poor soils cause the same symptom; at large scale it cuts agricultural productivity.

definition.text: Ways of preventing or reversing soil acidification, chiefly lime, organic amendments and biochar, with careful fertilizer and irrigation management.

facts.text: Liming acidic soils under sugarcane, soybean and corn restored nutrients, raised pH, increased root biomass and improved plant health.
Liming deeper in the soil works better than surface liming but is costlier and harder.
Prevention includes less acidifying fertilizers, timing them to cut nitrate leaching, irrigating with acid-neutralising water and weighing basic nutrients against nitrogen removed in crops.
Sulfur fertilizers should be used only on responsive crops with a high rate of crop recovery.

definition.text: The salt content of a soil; the process by which it increases is called salinization.

facts.text: The ions responsible for salinization are Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and Cl−.
Salts come from mineral weathering, dust and precipitation; with enough rain they are leached away, but under intense evaporation they rise by capillarity and gather near the surface.
Salts accumulate naturally in dry regions, as in large parts of Australia.
Human causes include irrigation, road salt and disrupted drainage; after Egypt's Aswan High Dam was built in 1970, a persistently high water table salinized arable land.
Increasing aridity from human-induced global warming also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils.
Salinity is an important land degradation problem: it harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks, pipes and cables, and degrades water quality.
It can be reduced by leaching salts out with excess good-quality irrigation water, combined with water-table control and subsurface drainage.
Calcium counters salinity, easing effects such as reduced water uptake by plants.

definition.text: A soil in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations.

facts.text: Sodic soils may be acidic, neutral or alkaline in pH.
They tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage; where clays are saturated with sodium the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away.
They tend to form columnar peds near the surface.
They can accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants.
Gypsum is the most common reclamation compound, and salt-tolerant organisms such as halophytes and halophilic rhizobacteria may help.
The term is used loosely, often interchangeably with alkali soil, defined as pH above 8.2, exchangeable sodium above 15% of CEC, or both.

definition.text: Salt build-up in irrigated soils, because nearly all water carries dissolved salts that stay behind in the root zone when plants use the water.

facts.text: Salinization occurs where evaporation concentrates dissolved salts in the root zone faster than drainage flushes them away.
Water applied beyond the plants' needs to carry salts away is called the leaching fraction.
Poor drainage and the use of saline water for irrigation greatly increase it.
In cities it often stems from watering gardens and recreation areas with salt-laden reclaimed water, combined with groundwater processes.
Good irrigation management prevents it by supplying enough drainage water to leach the added salts.
Even water with a low salt content of 0.3 g/L, applied at a modest 10,000 m3/ha a year, brings 3,000 kg of salt per hectare each year.
Most irrigation water is saltier and applied more heavily, so irrigated areas often receive more than 3,000 kg/ha of salt a year, some as much as 10,000 kg/ha.
Waterlogging is the secondary cause: irrigation efficiency is at most about 70%, so 30% or more of the water goes underground, raising water tables that block leaching.

definition.text: Controlling salinization to prevent soil degradation, and reclaiming soils that are already saline.

facts.text: Irrigation is the main human cause of salinization, since river water and groundwater carry salts that stay in the soil after the water evaporates.
The main method is to let 10–20% of the irrigation water leach the soil and leave through a drainage system.
Where salinity is stable, drainage water is normally 5 to 10 times saltier than the irrigation water, so salt export matches salt import.
When salinized soil is reclaimed, drainage water may at first be 50 times saltier than irrigation water; after one or two years a new, favourable equilibrium is reached.
About 62 million hectares, 20% of the world's irrigated land, is salt-affected, up from 45 million ha in the early 1990s.
In the Indo-Gangetic Plain, yield losses on salt-affected land could be 40% for wheat, 45% for rice, 48% for sugarcane and 63% for cotton.
Salinization normally affects 20% to 30% of the land in irrigation projects; depressions in undulating land degrade the most.
Salty drainage water can harm areas downstream, so drainage is best limited to wet seasons when possible.

title: Measuring soil salinity

definition.text: Determining soil salinity as the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or as its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m.

facts.text: The two units relate by about 5/3: y g/L corresponds to 5y/3 dS/m; seawater may hold 30 g/L (3%) with an EC of 50 dS/m.
The standard is the EC of an extract of a saturated soil paste, obtained by centrifugation and written ECe.
A 2:1 or 5:1 water:soil mixture is easier to measure, and ECe is about 4 times the EC of a 2:1 mixture.
Soils are saline when ECe > 4: slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, and severely saline above 16.
Sensitive crops lose vigour already in slightly saline soils, most crops suffer in moderately saline ones, and only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline soils.

notes: S:23bdead361ad writes the ratio as ECe = 4EC1:2 after naming the 2:1 mixture; the fact follows the 2:1 wording.

title: Leaching requirement

definition.text: The amount of water that must percolate through the root zone to keep soil salinity at a desired level, worked out from the salt balance.

facts.text: The water balance of the zone above the water table sets infiltration of rain and irrigation against evaporation, percolation to groundwater and capillary rise.
Leaching efficiency is often 0.7 to 0.8 but can be lower in poorly structured heavy clays; in Portugal's Leziria Grande polder it was only 0.15.
The desired soil salinity depends on the crop's tolerance to salt.
From it the irrigation and drainage needed for salinity control can be computed.

notes: how-soils-form also drafts Leaching requirement (Leaching model (soil)#Leaching requirement); merge the two, keeping this entry's salt-balance facts.; acidity-alkalinity-and-salinity also drafts Leaching requirement (Soil salinity control#Soil leaching); merge the two, keeping both entries' facts.

definition.text: Land drainage, usually by horizontal but also by vertical systems, that carries salty water away and lowers the water table.

facts.text: In many cases a seasonal average water table depth of 0.6 to 0.8 m is deep enough.
A fluctuating water table helps the soil breathe, expelling root carbon dioxide and drawing in oxygen.
A not-too-deep water table discourages over-irrigation, since crop yields would fall as the water table rose.
Where wet and dry seasons are marked, running drains only in the wet season, called controlled drainage, saves irrigation water.

title: Strip cropping for salinity control
article: Soil salinity control#Strip cropping: an alternative

definition.text: Irrigating alternate strips of land and leaving those between permanently fallow, so the fallow strips drain and absorb salt from the cropped ones.

facts.text: The irrigated strips have a higher water table that pushes groundwater toward the unirrigated strips, acting as subsurface drainage and allowing leaching.
In the dry, sacrificial strips groundwater rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts, so these strips salinize.
The sacrificial strips can carry livestock, salt-resistant grasses or deep-rooted salt-tolerant trees such as Casuarina, Eucalyptus or Atriplex, or be used for salt harvesting.

definition.text: Computer models of water and salt movement in soil used to predict salinity under irrigation and drainage.

facts.text: Most, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, combine Richards' equation for unsaturated water flow with Fick's convection–diffusion equation for salts.
They need hard-to-measure soil properties, short time steps and daily or hourly data, and are hard to calibrate because field salinity varies greatly.
Simpler models such as SaltMod use monthly or seasonal water and salt balances for long-term predictions, and SahysMod adds spatial variation with groundwater.

definition.text: An irrigation water quality index, calculated from sodium, calcium and magnesium concentrations, used in managing sodium-affected soils.

facts.text: It is also the standard diagnostic of a soil's sodicity hazard, measured on pore water extracted from the soil.
SAR = [Na+]/√([Ca2+]/2 + [Mg2+]/2), with concentrations in milliequivalents per litre.
Sodium and potassium disperse clay particles while calcium and magnesium flocculate them, so SAR shows whether clay aggregates will flocculate or disperse.
Years of irrigation with high-SAR water let sodium displace soil calcium and magnesium, ruining aggregate stability, structure and tilth and reducing infiltration and permeability.
Below an SAR of 3 there is no problem; above 9, fine-textured soils have severe problems, while sandy soils suffer less.
For irrigation the SAR should not be much above 20 and preferably below 10; after long exposure, a soil's ESP comes to roughly equal the water's SAR.
SAR addresses sodium only; the potassium adsorption ratio (PAR) and the cation ratio of structural stability (CROSS) extend it to other cations.

title: Exchangeable sodium percentage

definition.text: The share of a soil's exchangeable cations, and so of its cation-exchange capacity, that is sodium, expressed as a percentage.

facts.text: Calculated as sodium divided by total cations times 100, it is a key indicator of dispersive soils.
High sodium makes wet particles repel one another, so soils with a high ESP lose structure as their aggregates disperse.
Clay with an ESP above 16 in contact with non-saline water has an expanded double layer, so the soil swells and disperses.
Applying gypsum lowers ESP by displacing sodium with calcium.
Clays with an ESP near 100%, almost fully sodium-saturated, are called bentonite and are used to make impermeable curtains below dams.

notes: No article of its own; named on Alkali soil, Dispersion (geology), Gypsum, Soil structure and Soil salinity.

definition.text: A clay soil with a high pH, generally above 8.5, often with poor structure and low infiltration capacity.

facts.text: Its poor properties come mainly from sodium carbonate, which makes the soil swell and hard to settle; such soils are also called alkaline sodic soils.
Alkali soils often have a hard calcareous layer 0.5 to 1 metre beneath the surface.
Alkalinity comes from sodium carbonate and bicarbonate, released by weathering of soil minerals or brought in by irrigation and flood water.
Na2CO3 is about 78000 times more soluble than CaCO3, so it can push pH above 8.5, the most calcium carbonate in equilibrium with dissolved carbon dioxide allows.
As Ca2+ precipitates, clays take up Na+ and their ESP rises; above an ESP of 16 they swell and disperse, crusting and compacting the topsoil and cutting infiltration.
Alkalinity is worse in clay soils, especially swelling montmorillonite or smectite clays, and alkaline soils are in principle not saline, since alkalinity worsens as salinity falls.
Rainwater stagnates and evaporates on the surface, so farming is mostly limited to crops tolerant of waterlogging, such as rice.
Irrigation with softened water, its calcium and magnesium replaced by sodium, dissolves organic matter and disperses clay, giving the structure typical of alkali soils.

conflicts.text: Alkali soil defined as having a pH greater than 8.2 (or exchangeable sodium above 15% of CEC).
conflicts.note: Soil salinity puts the alkali-soil pH threshold at 8.2; Alkali soil says generally above 8.5.

definition.text: Soil alkalinity caused by people, mainly through sodium salts and lime that reach soil in irrigation water, effluent and industrial emissions.

facts.text: Fly ash from coal-fired boilers contains calcium oxide, which dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, and is carried by runoff into rivers and irrigation systems.
Lime softening precipitates Ca2+ and Mg2+ from water and converts its sodium bicarbonate into sodium carbonate.
Sodium from industrial and household salts enters surface water and groundwater; global sodium chloride consumption was 280 million tons in 2020.
Sodium salt loads are worst downstream in intensively cultivated river basins, where salts concentrate in the water left after transpiration and evaporation.

definition.text: Improving alkali soils by supplying calcium or acidifying material to replace or neutralise excess sodium, and leaching the sodium away.

facts.text: Gypsum supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex and turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulphate.
Enough natural or artificial subsurface drainage is needed for rain or irrigation water to leach the excess sodium.
Acidifying minerals such as pyrite, alum or aluminium sulfate, calcium chloride, calcium nitrate and spent acids can also be used.
Soils with solid CaCO3 can be reclaimed with grass, compost and other organic waste that adds acidifying material and releases CO2 to dissolve calcium.
Efforts usually target the top 10 cm, and treatments need repeating in about 5 years as amendments leach or decompose.
Halophytes such as glasswort, saltwort or barilla absorb sodium carbonate into their tissues, a form of phytoremediation; their ash yields soda.
Saline soils are mostly also sodic but keep good structure, so leaching does not usually turn them into alkali soils and they mostly need no gypsum.

title: Saline-alkali aquaculture
article: Alkali soil#Remediation and utilization via aquaculture

definition.text: Using fish and seafood farming on saline-alkali land to leach salts, add organic matter and put non-arable land to use.

facts.text: Research and experiments in China and elsewhere since the 1990s have combined agriculture and aquaculture on alkali land with considerable success.
Farmed species include shrimps, crabs, shellfish and fish such as sea bass and grouper, raised in inland saline-alkali water.
China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs recommends it as an economically viable and environmentally beneficial way to use saline-alkali land.

definition.text: An index of the alkalinity hazard that irrigation water or soil water poses to soil.

facts.text: It judges irrigation water for clay soils with a high cation-exchange capacity, where sodium high relative to calcium and magnesium makes clay swell or disperse and infiltration collapse.
RSC = (HCO3− + CO32−) − (Ca2+ + Mg2+) in meq/L; for irrigation it should not be much above 1 and preferably below 0.5.
Unlike saline water, high-RSC water does not raise osmotic pressure against root uptake, but irrigating clay soils with it creates fallow alkali soils.
Soda ash from weathered basalt, lime from burnt calcareous coal, and industrial soda ash raise river water RSC, often making lower reaches unfit for irrigation.

definition.text: Salinity in unirrigated landscapes: a rise in the salt of soil, water or the wider environment beyond normal levels, natural but greatly worsened by human activity.

facts.text: It results from groundwater recharge, movement and discharge; clearing deep-rooted plants lets excess water seep past the root zone and the water table rises.
Capillary action then brings salt to the surface; this happens when the water table is two to three metres down in clayey soils but less than a metre in sandy ones.
Clearing as little as 25% of a catchment can cause salinity, and in many Australian landscapes aquifer capacity is orders of magnitude below the altered recharge.
Native vegetation forms a 'soil sponge' of roots and soil up to 6 metres deep that keeps the water table low; shallow-rooted crops such as wheat thin it to 1 metre or less.
Salts accumulate where evaporation outpaces rainfall's replenishment of groundwater, as in arid environments.
Saline groundwater discharge cuts farm production, degrades natural environments and surface water, damages roads and leads to soil erosion.
Restoring the balance needs deep-rooted vegetation such as mallee eucalyptus or perennial grasses, or farming adapted to shallow saline groundwater.

definition.text: The division of salinity into primary salinity, which is natural, and secondary salinity, which human activity induces.

facts.text: Primary salinity occurs naturally in arid and saline settings such as salt lakes, marshes, pans and salt flats, left by past cycles of drainage, desiccation and sea winds.
Secondary salinity results directly from development, agriculture and irrigation, harming biodiversity and land productivity.
Secondary salinisation can make soils dispersive, so excess salt also needs managing at landscape scale.

definition.text: Reducing dryland salinity by cutting groundwater recharge through soils and vegetation, and coping with salt where groundwater discharges.

facts.text: Soils take up water by their field capacity and starting dryness, so the drier a soil enters winter, the more water it can store instead of leaking to groundwater.

Cutting recharge to pre-clearing levels is usually infeasible because too few profitable perennials can replace crops, so the aim is to minimise it with alley farming, perennials and winter–spring leaf cover.
In discharge areas salinity is managed with salt-tolerant plants or with engineering such as deep open drains, pumps and siphons.
Recharge is also the source of fresh groundwater, so its use must be traded off against salinity.

definition.text: A seep of saline water where alkali salt crystals form as the salty water reaches the surface and evaporates.

facts.text: Seeps form by capillary rise from a water table below the surface or where a water table flows out at the surface.
Saline discharge areas are called seeps where groundwater meets the soil surface, and scalds where water is lost by evaporation only.
They harm agriculture by reducing yields and restricting growth, yet host salt-adapted and often endemic organisms.

title: Salinity in Australia

definition.text: Soil salinity and dryland salinity as problems degrading the environment of Australia.

facts.text: Most states are affected, above all south-west Western Australia, which holds around 70% of Australia's salt-affected land.
Australian soils naturally hold salt gathered over thousands of years from ocean winds, evaporated inland seas and weathered parent rocks.
Before British settlement in 1788 groundwater levels were in equilibrium, as deep-rooted native vegetation used groundwater year-round.
Land clearing replaced that vegetation with crops and pasture; rising groundwater then brings stored salt up, and evaporation leaves it in the soil.
By 1999 about 2.5 million hectares had become salinised since European farming began; 5.7 million hectares now have high potential, expected to reach 17 million by 2050.
Salt cuts plants' water uptake by osmosis, burns leaves through sodium and chloride and upsets nutrient balance; it also damages roads, buildings, pipes and cables.
In the Murray River valley irrigation has caused salinity, while near Werrimull in Victoria land clearing did.
Predictions for climate change are mixed: lower rainfall may reduce salinity, but heavier downpours may add excess water to aquifers.

notes: Country-specific, but its own article and a frame seed; kept as the subject's main regional case of dryland salinity.

title: Australian salinity programs

definition.text: Australia's government and community programs for managing salinity at national, regional, state and farm level.

facts.text: Since 1983 governments have run the National Soil Conservation Program, National Landcare Program, Natural Heritage Trust, National Action Plan for Salinity and Water Quality and Caring for our Country.
The National Action Plan for Salinity and Water Quality ran from 2000 to 2008, with $1.4 billion committed over seven years.
Volunteer Landcare groups raised awareness of dryland salinity, while Saltwatch, begun in Victoria in 1987, has schools and communities monitor salinity in waterways.
There is no clear agreement on best practice; options include salt-tolerant plants, perennial crops and pastures, and deep drainage and pumping to lower groundwater.

notes: Country-specific programs without global significance; drafted from a seed's section but excluded by the country rule.

title: Acid sulfate soil

definition.text: Soils, sediments or organic substrates such as peat, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly pyrite, or their oxidation products.

facts.text: Undisturbed below the water table they are benign, but when drained, excavated or exposed to air their sulfides react with oxygen to form sulfuric acid.
Drained, they can become extremely acidic (pH < 4), and the acid releases iron, aluminium and other metals and metalloids, particularly arsenic.
The acid and metals kill vegetation and fish, acidify groundwater and surface water, and degrade concrete and steel structures to the point of failure.
Those most prone formed within the last 10,000 years, after the last major sea level rise mixed seawater sulfate with land sediments rich in iron oxides and organic matter.
They are widespread around coasts; in Australia coastal acid sulfate soils cover an estimated 58,000 km2 beneath estuaries and floodplains.
Dredging and dewatering for canal, housing and marina developments often disturb them, and droughts can expose them too; some drained 100 years ago still release acid.
Potential acid sulfate soils, or cat-clays, are often left uncultivated or planted with rice to keep them wet, and subsurface drainage is normally not advisable.
The term was coined for the first International Symposium on Acid Sulfate Soils, held in 1972 at Wageningen.

distinct_from: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils

title: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils
article: Acid sulfate soil#Generalised Pyrite Oxidation Reaction

definition.text: The oxidation of pyrite in drained soils to sulfuric acid and iron(III) hydroxide, which can make the soil extremely acidic.

facts.text: The overall reaction is 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O → 16H+ + 8SO42− + 4Fe(OH)3.
The orange iron(III) hydroxide precipitates and locks up the alkalinity, while the acidity stays active as sulfuric acid.
The acidity frees large amounts of Al3+ from clay minerals, harmful to vegetation, and leaves hydrogen clay, which is stable but poor in nutrients.
Other products include hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, hematite, goethite and iron sulfates such as jarosite, so these soils range from black and blue-gray to red, orange and yellow.

title: Sulfidic and sulfuric material
article: Acid sulfate soil#Sulfidic and Sulfuric Material

definition.text: Diagnostic materials of acid sulfate soils: sulfidic material holds detectable inorganic sulfides, and sulfuric material has a pH below 4 from their oxidation.

facts.text: Sulfidic material holds at least 0.01% sulfidic sulfur in layers at least 30 mm thick, and is divided into hyposulfidic, hypersulfidic and monosulfidic classes.
Hypersulfidic material would fall below pH 4 if exposed to oxidising conditions and hyposulfidic would not, though its weathering still yields saline solutions with hazardous metals.
Coined mainly by Fanning, Rabenhorst and Fitzpatrick, the terms are diagnostic features in the Australian Soil Classification and the World Reference Base.
The term 'self-neutralising' acid sulfate soil is discouraged because it suggests the soil is not hazardous.

related: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
distinct_from: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils

title: Acid base accounting

definition.text: The practice of quantifying the sources of acidity and alkalinity in acid sulfate soils so they can be managed.

facts.text: It is used, for example, to work out how much lime is needed to neutralise sulfidic material dug up or dredged.
Net acidity is potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralising capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil.

Potential sulfidic acidity measures oxidisable reduced inorganic sulfur such as iron sulfides; the chromium reducible sulfur test measures it without interference from sulfate minerals or organic matter.
Samples oxidise rapidly in air, so they should be cooled below 4°C at once, and monosulfidic samples frozen.

distinct_from: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils
notes: Anchored on the parent heading: the deepest heading, Overview, also names a section under Australian Guidance on the same page.

title: Managing acid sulfate soils

definition.text: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet, restoring their water table or neutralising their acid to prevent or repair acidification.

facts.text: On a Malaysian oil palm estate, yields fell from 17 tons of fresh fruit per ha in 1960 to 2 in 1965 after drainage was deepened in 1962, recovering after the water table was raised in 1966.
Aggressive drainage of potentially acid sulfate soils in the second half of the 20th century had disastrous results: barren land and clear, lifeless water.
Where soils cannot be kept wet, surface drainage in rainy periods removes acids formed in dry spells and can reclaim the soil in the long run.
When Australia's millennium drought exposed them, a bund, pumping and aerial limestone dosing were used to stop acidification of the Lower Lakes.

distinct_from: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils
notes: The oil palm yield table (S:cc56654d2aef) lists one value per year from 1960 to 1971: 17, 14, 15, 12, 8, 2, 4, 8, 14, 19, 18, 19.

title: Calcareous soil

definition.text: Soil formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite.

facts.text: Calcareous soils are relatively alkaline because their parent material contains calcium carbonate, and the carbonate ion is a base.
They may have a calcic horizon of secondary carbonates, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.
Calcareous grassland grows on soils rich in calcium carbonate from underlying chalk or limestone.
Calcisols are common on calcareous parent materials in arid and semi-arid environments, and loess is often calcareous.
In such low-acidity soils, earthworms mix humus with the underlying mineral soil to form mull humus.

notes: The Calcareous page is a general adjective article; only its soil section is used.

definition.text: A soil accumulation of calcium carbonate at depth, where it precipitates and binds other materials such as gravel, sand, clay and silt.

facts.text: It occurs worldwide in aridisols and mollisols of arid and semiarid regions, such as central and western Australia, the Kalahari and the High Plains of the western United States.
Also called calcrete or kankar, it forms layers from a few inches to feet thick, sometimes called a K horizon.
It forms where annual precipitation is under 65 centimeters and mean annual temperature exceeds 5 °C; wetter climates leach the calcium away.
Root carbon dioxide in the A horizon, up to 15 times atmospheric levels, dissolves calcium carbonate as bicarbonate, which reverts to carbonate in the less active B horizon.
Its depth follows rainfall: about 25 centimeters down at 35 centimeters of rain a year, about 125 centimeters at 75, and gone above 100 centimeters.
Deposition takes several thousand years, and the calcium can arrive as aeolian dust even over calcium-poor bedrock.
Impermeable caliche blocks drainage and roots, and the basic soil it creates can cause iron deficiency that yellows the youngest leaves.
Caliches store significant carbon, mattering to the global carbon cycle, and calcretes in the geologic record preserve past climates.

definition.text: Vast deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert, also called caliche, of gypsum, sodium chloride, other salts and sand together with nitrate minerals (salitre).

facts.text: Salitre is sodium and potassium nitrate; the deposits average 7.5% sodium nitrate, with sodium sulfate, sodium chloride, borate, iodine and perchlorate.
Salitre earned Chile important export revenue until the early 1930s, when Europe began making nitrates industrially in large quantities.
Caliche is Chile's main iodine ore, and the country hosts over half the world's iodine reserves.
Its origin is unclear: an evaporated prehistoric inland sea and weathering of the Andes are both proposed.

definition.text: A hardened soil layer made of around 95% gypsum (calcium sulfate).

facts.text: It is the arid-climate counterpart of calcrete, which cannot form in very arid climates.
Gypcrust horizons can be up to 5 m thick with 75–97% gypsum, mostly where annual rainfall averages under 250 mm, since gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches under higher rainfall.
It forms in three stages: crystallisation from surface brines or groundwater, transport and redeposition by wind or water, and alteration above or below the capillary fringe.
Gypsum cements are rarely as strong as calcretes or silcretes, though gypcrete has been used for road construction in the Sahara.

definition.text: A hard layer on or near the soil surface where soluble minerals have precipitated and hardened.

facts.text: Duricrusts range from a few millimeters or centimeters to several meters thick; the general term is not to be confused with duripan.
They form as mineral-bearing waters moving up, down or sideways by capillary action deposit soluble minerals, often helped by evaporation in arid settings.

Types are named by dominant mineral: ferricrete (laterite) iron sesquioxides, alcrete (bauxite) aluminium sesquioxides, silcrete silica, calcrete (caliche) calcium carbonate and gypcrete (gypcrust) gypsum.
In the per ascensum model, evaporation draws solutions up from a shallow water table to form thin crusts; in the per descensum model, downward-percolating solutions build thick ones.
Duricrust found at the Viking 2 and Phoenix landing sites on Mars, the latter confirmed water-based, may help show the planet once had more water.

definition.text: A computer program that predicts salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, water table depth and drain discharge in irrigated land, mapping spatial variation with a network of polygons.

facts.text: Developed by the Institute for Land Reclamation and Improvement (ILRI), it was designed for field technicians, engineers and planners rather than specialised geohydrologists.
It computes groundwater levels and flows between polygons by numerically solving the Boussinesq equation.
It runs on seasonal inputs and outputs, with one to four seasons a year, and up to 240 internal and 120 external polygons.
Salt balances are computed for each soil reservoir separately, and farmers' responses to waterlogging and salinity can be built in.

definition.text: The changes irrigation makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water, and their effects on natural and social conditions in river basins and downstream.

facts.text: Direct effects include reduced downstream river flow, more evaporation in the irrigated area and a rising water table from increased groundwater recharge.
Slower but longer-lasting indirect effects include waterlogging, soil salination, ecological damage and socioeconomic impacts.
Deep percolation losses are commonly 40% to 60%, raising water tables; where tables are shallow, less water is applied, the soil is no longer leached and salinity develops.
Over-irrigation causes irrigation salinity through rising water tables, while under-irrigation also raises salinity by failing to flush out salts.
About one-third of irrigated land in the major irrigation countries is or soon will be badly salt-affected: estimates are 13% in Israel, 20% in Australia, 15% in China, 50% in Iraq and 30% in Egypt.
Irrigated land covers about 16% of the world's agricultural area but gives roughly 40% of total crop yield.
Pumping wells beyond recharge mines groundwater and can cause land subsidence and, on coasts, saltwater intrusion.
Stagnant water tables at the surface raise the incidence of water-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis.

title: Framboid

definition.text: A raspberry-like microscopic structure common in some sedimentary minerals, especially pyrite: a roughly spherical cluster of tiny crystals.

facts.text: Clusters average 5-20 μm across and are built of regular microcrystals around 0.5 μm in diameter; the name, first used by Rust in 1935, comes from French 'framboise', raspberry.
In acid sulfate soils, bacteria such as Desulfovibrio desulfuricans reduce sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, which reacts with ferrous iron to form fine, highly reactive framboidal pyrite.
Framboidal pyrite is common in coastal sediments such as marsh soils, estuarine sediments and beach sands; greigite is considered an essential precursor.
Once thought to be fossil bacterial colonies, framboids have since been made in the laboratory and found in places hostile to microbial life.

related: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils

definition.text: A mathematical model of how crop yield responds to soil salinity, drawn as a horizontal line that breaks into a downward slope.

facts.text: The breakpoint, or tolerance, is the salinity up to which yield is unaffected; beyond it yield falls.
Yield Y equals the maximum C below the breakpoint Pb and AX + B above it, where X is soil salinity, A the slope and B the regression constant.
Pb is found by regression and optimisation for the best fit, but a flat tail in the data can give a misleadingly low breakpoint.
An inverted form serves factors such as water table depth that cut yields only at low values.

title: Agricultural gypsum

definition.text: Gypsum (calcium sulfate) applied to soil as a fertilizer and amendment, supplying calcium and sulfur without generally changing soil pH.

facts.text: It is used to reclaim saline and sodic soils regardless of pH, lowering the exchangeable sodium percentage.
In sodic and acidic soils it turns soluble sodium metaborate into less soluble calcium metaborate and reduces aluminium and boron toxicity.
It also improves soil structure, water absorption and aeration.
In the late 18th and early 19th centuries Nova Scotia gypsum, called plaster, was a sought-after fertilizer for US wheat fields.

notes: The Gypsum page is crawled but sits in no chapter's dossier; drafted from its agriculture section because gypsum is the standard sodic-soil amendment.

definition.text: A salt-tolerant plant that grows in soils or waters of high salinity, such as salt marshes, mangroves and saline semi-deserts.

facts.text: Perhaps only 2% of plant species are halophytes; most are glycophytes, which high salinity damages fairly easily.
By dissolved solids in irrigation water, beans and rice tolerate about 1–3 g/L, barley and date palm about 5 g/L, and Salicornia bigelovii grows well at 70 g/L.
Iversen (1936) grouped them by soil NaCl: oligo-halophytes at 0.01 to 0.1%, meso-halophytes at 0.1 to 1%, and euhalophytes above 1%.
Halophytes such as Suaeda salsa store salt ions taken from soil, so they can lower soil salinity enough for glycophytes to grow again.

title: Pyrite

definition.text: Iron sulfide, FeS2, the most common sulfide mineral, also known as fool's gold.

facts.text: It occurs in igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks and is common in shale, where it precipitates from anoxic seawater, and in coal beds.
Exposed to oxygen and water it breaks down into iron oxyhydroxides and sulfuric acid, a reaction sped up by Acidithiobacillus bacteria.
Finely dispersed framboidal pyrite, formed by sulfate-reducing bacteria in clayey sediments, oxidizes faster.
Its oxidation causes acid mine drainage; limestone dust spread in coal mines neutralizes the acid and slows the oxidation.

related: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils

definition.text: Growing plants with saline groundwater or on saline soil, using salt-tolerant plants to farm land too salty for ordinary crops.

facts.text: Halophytes are its cornerstone, used for food and forage, restoring salty land, medicine and biofuel.
Irrigating with high-salinity water eases pressure on scarce fresh water, especially in arid and semi-arid regions with brackish or saline sources.
Soil salinization affects an estimated one billion hectares worldwide, with another one million hectares added each year.
Salinity affects one quarter of global arable land and is projected to double by 2050.
Repeated cycles of halophyte growth can restore degraded soil and water; the plants also accumulate heavy metals from soils and groundwater.
Salinity troubles date back to Mesopotamia, where widespread soil salinization from poor irrigation helped bring the civilizations down, from 2400 BC to 1700 BC.
The field was formalized in the late 1990s, with the International Center for Biosaline Agriculture founded in 1996.

definition.text: The ability of an organism to live in salt concentrations above those it needs for growth.

facts.text: Halotolerant bacteria, archaea and fungi live in saline waters and soils; unlike halophiles they do not need high salinity.
High salt in soil or water upsets ionic balance, impairing respiration and photosynthesis and slowing growth or killing sensitive plants.
Salinity places both osmotic and ionic stress on cells, which drives water out, so tolerant organisms retain water and sequester salt.
Halotolerant bacteria can remediate saline soil by lowering its sodium content and sodium adsorption ratio and by degrading toxic compounds.

definition.text: A quantitative estimate of pollutant exposure below which significant harm to specified sensitive parts of the environment does not occur, as far as is known.

facts.text: Work has centred on sulfur and nitrogen deposition, both of which can acidify soils and surface waters.
As acidifying agents they can strip calcium from soil and release toxic aluminium, harming plants and animals.
Deposition above the critical load is an exceedance, putting the biota at greater risk of ecological harm.

In Europe a sensitive element is tied to a chemical criterion, such as the soil base cation to aluminium ratio with a limit of Bc/Al = 1, and a mass balance model gives the deposition that reaches it.
Today a two-dimensional critical load function is often calculated, with nitrogen deposition on one axis and sulfur deposition on the other.
It is a steady-state concept that says nothing about how long effects take to appear; target load functions add a time dimension.
Empirical critical loads come from observed ecosystem responses, while steady-state mass balance ones come from models that can include soil chemistry and mineral weathering rates.

definition.text: An inverted S-curve relating crop yield to soil salinity.

facts.text: It is named after Martinus Theodore van Genuchten and Satyandra K. Gupta, from their work in the 1990s.
Yield is Y = Ym / (1 + (C/C50)^P), where Ym is maximum yield, C the soil salt concentration, C50 the concentration giving 50% yield and P a fitted exponent.
A logistic S-function or a cubic regression of yield on soil salt concentration can be used instead.

definition.text: The salt spread on roads and walkways to melt ice, and its build-up in roadside soils and waters.

facts.text: Sodium chloride is the most common form; calcium and magnesium chlorides are used too, especially in colder weather.
Millions of tons are applied to roads each year, making it one of the most widely used chemicals in urban infrastructure.
Chloride from road salt persists in soils, surface waters and groundwater, harming aquatic life, roadside vegetation and drinking water.
Salt build-up in roadside soils raises their salinity, hindering plant growth, killing sensitive species and adding to soil erosion.

definition.text: The movement of saline water into freshwater aquifers, degrading groundwater quality.

facts.text: It occurs naturally in coastal aquifers: denser saline water pushes inland beneath the fresh water.
Pumping from coastal freshwater wells lowers the fresh groundwater's pressure and lets saltwater flow further inland.
Agricultural and drainage channels, sea level rise and storm surges also drive it.
Seawater intrusion into rivers can harm agriculture in upstream areas.

definition.text: The capacity of water to resist acidification, set by its buffer of weak acids and their conjugate bases.

facts.text: It is not the same as basicity, which is an absolute position on the pH scale.
It is measured by titrating with an acid such as HCl to an endpoint, and expressed in units such as meq/L or mg/L as CaCO3.
Alkalinity is low in freshwater on non-limestone terrain and is one of the best measures of a stream's sensitivity to acid inputs.
Acid rain from SOx and NOx emissions can change the alkalinity of streams and rivers over the long term.

definition.text: A measure of how well a solution of ions conducts electricity, used to gauge how much dissolved salt it holds.

facts.text: Its SI unit is the siemens per metre (S/m).
Measuring it is a fast, cheap and reliable way to find a solution's ionic content, and it is often linked directly to total dissolved solids.
Typical drinking water runs 200–800 μS/cm, while sea water is about 50 mS/cm.

definition.text: Poisoning of plants by manganese that becomes soluble at low soil pH.

facts.text: With aluminium toxicity it is a serious problem in Alisols, whose low pH makes normally insoluble metals soluble enough to poison intolerant plants.
It may occur in strongly acidic horizons, especially when they are waterlogged.
Liming with finely ground limestone or dolomite to bring acid soil near neutral reduces aluminium and manganese toxicity.

definition.text: A theory of acids and bases in which an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor.

facts.text: When an acid and a base react, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base becomes its conjugate acid by exchanging a proton (H+).
The theory was proposed independently in 1923 by Brønsted in Denmark and Lowry in England, and it generalises the Arrhenius theory.
Acetic acid donates a proton to water and becomes acetate; water accepts it and becomes the hydronium ion. Unlike Arrhenius theory, an acid need not dissociate.
An acid is only an acid relative to a base. Water is amphoteric, acting as acid or base, and aluminium hydroxide also reacts with both OH− and H+.
Lewis theory, from the same year, defines a base as an electron-pair donor and an acid as an electron-pair acceptor, and explains the Brønsted–Lowry classification through electronic structure.
Metal aqua cations behave as acids in Brønsted–Lowry terms.

definition.text: A solution whose pH changes little on dilution or when a small amount of strong acid or base is added.

facts.text: A buffer resists pH change through the equilibrium between a weak acid HA and its conjugate base A−; added acid shifts the equilibrium toward HA (Le Chatelier's principle), so hydrogen ion concentration rises less than expected.
Added alkali likewise lowers hydrogen ion concentration by less than the amount expected.
The buffer region lies at pH = pKa ± 1, centred where [HA] = [A−]; once the acid is more than 95% deprotonated, pH rises rapidly.
Buffer capacity measures the strong acid or base needed to change the pH of a given volume by a given amount; it is highest when a large addition produces only a small pH change.
Capacity considers a macroscopic change of 1 pH unit, whereas the buffer index considers an infinitesimal change.
Polyprotic acids have several pKa values; when successive values differ by less than about 3 their ranges overlap, so citric acid buffers across pH 2.5 to 7.5.
A buffer can be made by mixing an acid with its conjugate base, such as acetic acid with sodium acetate, or by adding strong acid or base to a buffering agent.
Cation-exchange capacity is often measured with a buffer solution at a set pH, and fens keep a stable pH through bicarbonate buffering.

title: Efflorescence

definition.text: The migration of a salt to the surface of a porous material, where it forms a coating.

facts.text: Water dissolves a salt held inside, carries it to the surface and evaporates, leaving a salt coating. It occurs in natural and built environments.
In primary efflorescence the water is the invader and the salt was already inside; in secondary efflorescence salt from outside is carried in solution into the material.
Salt crystals can clog pores and destroy the material through internal water pressure, as in the spalling of brick.

notes: Wikipedia page is mostly about masonry; only the general mechanism is used.

definition.text: Two intrinsic properties of a material that measure its ability to conduct electric current; each is the reciprocal of the other.

facts.text: Resistivity (ρ) has the SI unit ohm-metre; conductivity (σ) has the SI unit siemens per metre.
In a uniform conductor, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, with resistivity as the constant of proportionality.
Resistivity and conductivity are intensive properties; resistance and conductance are the matching extensive properties of a specific object.
In electrolytes, current is carried by travelling ions. Resistivity varies tremendously with concentration: distilled water is almost an insulator, salt water a reasonable conductor.
A metal has high conductivity and low resistivity; an insulator such as glass has low conductivity and high resistivity.
Resistivity of metals generally rises with temperature, while that of intrinsic semiconductors falls.

definition.text: The minimum pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop its pure solvent flowing in across a semipermeable membrane.

facts.text: Osmosis happens when solutions of different solute concentration are separated by a selectively permeable membrane; solvent moves toward the higher-concentration side until osmotic equilibrium.
Van 't Hoff related osmotic pressure to solute concentration: Π = i c R T for low-concentration ideal solutions, so it is a colligative property.
In a hypotonic environment a cell takes in water; in plant cells the wall resists, creating turgor pressure that holds herbaceous plants upright and regulates stomata.
Reverse osmosis applies pressure above the osmotic pressure to purify water; ocean water is about 27 atm.

definition.text: Well-humified organic matter and clay minerals together supply a soil's cation exchange capacity, and the organic share can be estimated from pH and organic matter content.

facts.text: A soil's total CEC is the sum of the CEC due to organic matter and that due to clays; in fine soils with medium to high-CEC clays most of it is clay-based.
In sandy loams with little clay, and in southeastern US and tropical soils with low-CEC clays, organic matter may supply most of the CEC.
CEC is expressed as milliequivalents of negative charge per 100 g of soil.
Rule of thumb: for every pH unit above 4.5, organic matter gives 1 me of CEC per 100 g of soil for each percent of organic matter; at pH 6 and 3% organic matter this is 4.5 me/100 g.

definition.text: Copper is sometimes deficient in high-pH soils and in organic soils.

facts.text: It can also be deficient in organic soils with 10-20% or more organic matter; tomatoes, lettuce, beets, onions and spinach have relatively high copper needs.
Copper sulfate and copper chelates correct a deficiency.
Most soil sulfur is in organic matter, so maintaining organic matter usually supplies enough; deficiency is likelier on acidic sandy soils and cold, dry spring soils with slow mineralization.
Deficiency is spreading in places as sulfur air pollution from coal falls, while Great Plains irrigation water may supply enough sulfur.

definition.text: Reserve acidity is the acid held on soil solids, mostly on organic matter and as aluminum, which dwarfs the acid in the soil water.

facts.text: Almost all of a soil's acid sits in reserve on the solids; only an extremely small amount is active in the soil water.
Neutralizing only the acid in the water would need a few handfuls of lime per acre, but raising pH takes tons per acre.
As H+ is removed from organic matter new CEC sites appear; as soils acidify, H+ takes over CEC sites and cuts their hold on calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium.
Alfalfa, from semiarid high-pH regions, needs pH 6.5-6.8 or higher; most states recommend about 6.8 only for the most sensitive crops and 6.2-6.5 for many clovers.

title: Saline soil management without shallow groundwater

definition.text: Where saline soils have no shallow salty groundwater, salinity is handled by keeping soil moist, growing tolerant crops and leaching.

facts.text: Keeping soil continually moist, as with low-salt drip irrigation plus mulch, stops salt concentrating as the soil dries.
Tolerant plants include barley, bermuda grass, oak, rosemary and willow, but only washing salt below the root zone removes it.
Poorly draining subsoil may need drainage tiles, which discharge salty water that can harm downstream water.
Seawater flooding after storm surges can make soils sodic, treated by gypsum, or lime where the soil is naturally acidic.
